blocks.text: Say you run a supplements brand and a creator posts a video saying your magnesium blend "cures insomnia". The video gets flagged, your ad account gets a warning, and you spend the next week explaining to a platform's review team why you didn't write that script.

This is the specific risk that makes supplement brands nervous about creator marketing. The category sells on real benefits, sleep, energy, digestion, recovery, but the words creators reach for naturally (cures, fixes, treats) are exactly the words that get content pulled and accounts restricted. The brands that grow through creators in this category aren't the ones avoiding the risk. They're the ones managing it.
What does creator marketing for supplement brands actually need to avoid?

The short answer: any language that implies a supplement diagnoses, treats, cures or prevents a disease, and any claim a creator can't personally back up. That covers phrases like "fixes my anxiety", "cured my acne" or "replaces my medication". It also covers subtler versions, a creator holding up a bottle next to a before-and-after photo, or captioning a video "this is why I stopped taking antidepressants".

None of this means creators can't talk about how a product made them feel. "I sleep better since I started taking this" is a personal observation. "This cures insomnia" is a medical claim. The line is between describing an experience and promising an outcome, and it needs to be drawn before filming starts, not fixed after the video is live.
How do you choose credible creators for a supplement brand?

Look for creators whose existing content already talks about the category honestly, someone who posts about their training, their skin, their sleep or their gut health as part of daily life, not someone who only posts sponsored hauls. A creator with a real relationship to wellness content is less likely to reach for a dramatic medical claim, because their audience already expects nuance from them.

Read a creator's last handful of posts before you approve them for a supplement campaign. Do they talk about their routine in specific, plausible terms, or in absolutes? Do they disclose sponsorships clearly? Have they made health claims for other brands before? A creator's history with other products in the category tells you more than their follower count ever will. [Micro creators](/blog/micro-influencers-for-ecommerce-brands) are often a safer fit here precisely because their content tends to be more personal and less performative.
How do you brief creators so they don't make medical claims?

Put the boundary in writing, not just in a call. A brief should give creators approved language for what the product does, a short list of phrases to avoid, and a note that says why: not "legal made us add this" but "we want your content to stay live and keep earning you money, and claims get videos pulled". Framing it as protecting their income, not policing their words, gets better compliance than a list of rules alone.

Give creators real detail to work with instead of vague guidance. Ingredients, how the product is meant to be used, what it's formulated to support, and one or two things it should not be described as doing. A [creator brief template](/blog/creator-brief-template-for-ecommerce) built for this level of detail saves you from reshoots and from the awkward conversation where you ask a creator to take a video down.
How do you frame benefits without crossing into medical claims?

Anchor benefit language to the person's own experience and to what the product is formulated to support, not to a guaranteed result. "Part of my evening routine" works. "Guaranteed to help you sleep" doesn't. "Formulated to support recovery after training" works. "Fixes soreness" doesn't. The pattern is always the same: describe intention and personal use, not promised outcomes.

This also protects the brand's tone. Supplement audiences are used to overclaiming and tend to trust brands that sound measured more than ones that sound miraculous. A creator saying "I've noticed I feel steadier through the afternoon since adding this" reads as credible in a way that a bold claim never will, and it's also the version that stays online.
How do you track results without relying on before-and-after claims?

Track content, reach, engagement and tracked sales per creator, the same as any other category, rather than leaning on testimonial-style proof to justify a campaign. A creator's unique link or code tells you whether their audience is buying without needing a dramatic claim to sell the story internally. On Linkable, that reporting sits alongside the content itself, so you can see which creators are driving orders and which are just producing nice video without needing to point to a claim as the reason it worked. If you haven't set this up yet, [how to measure creator marketing ROI](/blog/how-to-measure-creator-marketing-roi) covers the mechanics.

Deciding between gifted product and paid or affiliate terms matters more in this category than most, since a creator who's only being paid for reach has less reason to stick to approved language than one earning commission on tracked sales they want to keep generating. [Gifted vs paid creator collaborations](/blog/gifted-vs-paid-creator-collaborations) walks through how to pick.

This week, pull your last few pieces of supplement creator content and check the captions against the language you actually want tied to your brand. If you're setting up a new campaign, write the approved and avoided phrases into the brief before you send it, and [start the campaign on Linkable](/pricing) with that brief attached rather than adding it after the first video comes back.

faqs.a: It's safer to avoid naming specific conditions altogether. Creators should describe personal experience (how they feel, what they've noticed) rather than claiming the product treats or resolves a named condition.
faqs.q: Can creators mention specific health conditions when talking about supplements?

faqs.a: Creators earning commission on tracked sales have an ongoing incentive to keep their content live and their audience trusting them, which tends to make them more careful with language than a one-off gifted or flat-fee post.
faqs.q: Do gifted or paid creators make more claims than affiliates?

faqs.a: No. The risk comes from unclear briefs and unchecked creator history, not from creator marketing itself. Brands that brief clearly and choose creators with a credible track record in wellness content run these campaigns without issues.
faqs.q: Should supplement brands avoid working with creators entirely to reduce risk?

faqs.a: Ask for the content to be edited or removed straight away and follow up with a clearer brief for future posts. Treat it as a briefing gap to fix, not a reason to end the relationship, unless it happens repeatedly.
